mcqs.question: How does a Vision Transformer convert a 2D image into a format its Transformer encoder layers can process, given that Transformers were originally designed for sequences?
options: It runs the image through convolutional layers first to produce a sequence of feature maps
It converts each pixel individually into one token, with no patching step

It splits the image into fixed-size patches, flattens and linearly projects each into an embedding (analogous to a word embedding), adds positional encodings, and feeds the resulting sequence of patch tokens through standard Transformer blocks
It requires no conversion, since Transformer self-attention operates directly on raw 2D pixel grids
mcqs.explanation: ViT's key trick is treating fixed-size image patches as the "tokens" a Transformer expects, exactly paralleling how NLP Transformers treat subword tokens — patch, flatten, project, add position info, then standard self-attention. There's no convolutional layer in the core ViT architecture (A is false), using one token per pixel would be computationally prohibitive and isn't how ViT works (C is false), and self-attention requires a sequence input, so some conversion step is necessary (D is false).

mcqs.question: What specifically does a CNN's convolutional filter structure assume about images that a ViT does not assume by default?
options: That images must always be square, an assumption ViTs relax
That color images must be converted to grayscale before processing
That images contain exactly one object per frame

That nearby pixels tend to be related (locality) and the same feature detector is useful anywhere in the image (translation invariance) — assumptions baked into the architecture rather than learned from data
mcqs.explanation: Convolutional filters slide the same small set of weights across the whole image, structurally encoding the assumptions that local pixel patterns are meaningful (locality) and that a useful feature detector should work regardless of where in the image it appears (translation invariance) — ViT's global self-attention from the first layer makes no such built-in assumption and must learn any spatial structure from data. Image aspect ratio (A), object count per image (C), and color format (D) are unrelated to this inductive-bias distinction.

mcqs.question: A team trains a ViT from random initialization on 3,000 labeled images and finds it underperforms a comparably-sized CNN trained the same way. What is the most likely explanation, and what's the practical fix?
options: ViT lacks CNNs' built-in locality/translation-invariance assumptions, so it must learn spatial structure from data alone, which 3,000 images is often insufficient for; the fix is to fine-tune a pretrained ViT checkpoint instead of training from scratch
ViTs are strictly worse than CNNs at every dataset size; the fix is to always use a CNN
The CNN must have more parameters than the ViT, which is why it performed better
ViTs cannot be trained on datasets smaller than 1 million images under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: This is the well-documented small-data weakness of ViTs trained from scratch — without CNN-style inductive biases, they need to learn spatial relationships purely from examples, and a few thousand images is often not enough; the standard fix is to start from a large-scale pretrained ViT checkpoint and fine-tune, letting pretraining supply the spatial understanding. ViTs aren't strictly worse at every scale — they can surpass CNNs given enough pretraining data (A overclaims), the outcome isn't necessarily about parameter count (C), and ViTs absolutely can be fine-tuned (not trained from scratch) successfully well below 1 million images (D is false).

mcqs.question: In contrastive self-supervised pretraining for vision, what serves as the "label" that supervises training, given that no human annotations are used?
options: A pretrained classifier is used to generate pseudo-labels for each image before contrastive training begins
The image's file name or metadata is used as the supervisory signal
Whether two augmented views (crops, color jitter) came from the same original image or different images — this pairing information is free to generate at any scale without human annotation
Contrastive learning requires at least a small set of human labels to function at all
mcqs.explanation: The self-supervision comes entirely from knowing which augmented crops originated from the same source image — that pairing is trivially known at data-generation time and requires zero human labeling, and the training objective simply pulls same-image view embeddings together while pushing different-image view embeddings apart. There's no pseudo-labeling classifier involved (A), file metadata isn't used as a training signal (C), and the defining feature of this method is that it needs no human labels at all (D is false).

mcqs.question: A CLIP-style multimodal model can classify images into categories it was never explicitly trained to classify (zero-shot classification), just by comparing against text descriptions of candidate classes. What makes this possible?
options: The model memorizes every possible class name during pretraining
The model converts images to text captions first, then performs standard text classification
Zero-shot classification requires a separate fine-tuning step for every new class

Training on (image, caption) pairs with a contrastive objective produces a shared embedding space where matching image-text pairs are close together, so any candidate class's text embedding can be compared against an image's embedding without task-specific retraining
mcqs.explanation: The shared embedding space is the key mechanism: because the model was trained to place matching image-caption pairs near each other and mismatched pairs far apart across a huge and diverse set of pairs, any new class can be represented just by embedding its name as text and checking which class's text embedding is closest to the image's embedding, with no retraining needed. It isn't memorizing every class name (A), that's the opposite of what makes it zero-shot, no fine-tuning per new class is required (C is false, that would defeat the point of zero-shot), and CLIP-style models compare embeddings directly rather than first generating a caption and then classifying it (D is false).
